name: ALLFED (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a nuclear winter's famine would kill people everywhere, most in countries that import food, and the future lost is everyone's, so the result is spread by world population.
summary: ALLFED (the Alliance to Feed the Earth in Disasters) researches foods and food systems that could feed people after a catastrophe that blocks the sun or breaks the food supply, chiefly the famine after a nuclear war's soot cools the climate, and advises governments on plans for it; this model covers all its programmes in 2024 ($1.0M spent). At the defaults it averts about 26 years of healthy life per $1,000, from 0.9 to 750 on the combined range: each dollar is valued as a typical nuclear project's relative cut (Rethink Priorities' cross-cause model) applied not to the chance of a war but to the famine deaths if one comes (the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament's experts for the chance, Xia et al. 2022 for the famine), with a small part for food in an extreme pandemic and a share of an extinction-level war's future. The biggest uncertainty is how much a dollar of such work cuts those deaths: Rethink calls its figures placeholders, the range runs ten times either way, and they were not set with food resilience in mind; the result also moves with the years a cut counts and the discount rate. Both branches, nuclear winter and pandemics, are discounted for missing data: no food plan has been tested in a catastrophe.

rows.label: Pandemics: share of a catastrophe's deaths that come from the food supply failing
rows.explainer: ALLFED's pandemic work (begun in 2024, Part III line 4a; UK pandemic resilience planning, 4c) is on keeping food produced and delivered when a pandemic that kills over 10% of people keeps workers at home and breaks supply chains; it can avert only the deaths from hunger, not those from the disease. 10% (2% to 30%), our judgment: most deaths in such a pandemic are from the disease; the high end if, as in ALLFED's scenarios of an extreme pandemic, absenteeism stops farming, transport and power for months. The same share for an extinction-level pandemic would overstate, since that kills by disease: see bio_extinction_per_year.

rows.label: Pandemics: share of the extinction risk that runs through the food supply
rows.explainer: A pandemic that ends humanity's future would do so by killing nearly everyone with the disease; food reaching the survivors doesn't change that. 0 (0 to 5%), our judgment; the high end if a collapse of food and power after a very deadly pandemic stopped the survivors recovering.

rows.label: Pandemics: yearly chance of a smaller (COVID-scale) pandemic that breaks the food supply

The OECD's review of food supply chains in COVID-19 (https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/food-supply-chains-and-covid-19-impacts-and-policy-lessons_71b57aea-en.html) found food supply chains resilient and the main risk to food security people's access to food, not its availability. rows.label: Nuclear war: share of a catastrophe's deaths from famine
rows.explainer: The shared share of a nuclear war's deaths that come from famine after the soot cools the climate (Xia et al. 2022: 91% to 95% across the regional wars, as low as 60% if the winter is weaker than they model), the deaths resilient food can avert; blasts, fire and fallout ALLFED doesn't touch.

rows.label: Nuclear war: share of the extinction risk that runs through the food supply
rows.explainer: A nuclear war could end humanity's future mainly through what follows the blasts: a nuclear winter that starves nearly everyone, or a collapse the survivors never recover from. Blasts, fire and fallout kill far fewer than the famine (Xia et al. 2022's regional wars: 27 to 164 million direct deaths beside 0.26 to 2.5 billion from famine), so the extinction risk runs largely through food and the recovery of a starving world, the path ALLFED works on. But a soot load that cools the planet for a decade may be beyond what resilient foods can feed, and some of the risk is in a collapse of order that food alone doesn't fix. 30% (0 to 80%), our judgment; the low end 0 for those who think food work cannot touch an extinction-level war. At the default 4% discount rate this branch's future part is under a tenth of its value.

rows.label: Nuclear war: yearly chance of a smaller catastrophe
rows.explainer: A nuclear war that kills far less than 10% of people (Xia et al.'s smallest regional war starves 3.5% of people) has no shared forecast on the site; its famine, which ALLFED's work would also cut, is a named share in unmodelled_benefits_adj instead, so 0 here, as in the other nuclear models. Fixed at 0: no shared forecast of this size, not an uncertain estimate.

rows.explainer: Everyone alive × the shared share who die in a nuclear war the world survives (45%, from Xia et al.'s famine estimates) × the share of those deaths from famine (nuclear_famine_share): the deaths ALLFED's work is against. The typical $1 million's cut (nuclear_deaths_per_million) applies to these deaths: ALLFED doesn't change the chance of a war but the deaths if one comes, and a relative cut in the deaths given a war averts as many deaths as the same relative cut in its chance.

rows.label: Nuclear resilience work: share that wouldn't have been done anyway
rows.explainer: The share of the work no one else would have done now: few groups study feeding the world after a nuclear winter (the climate modellers behind Xia et al., a few university groups in New Zealand and elsewhere, national food-security planners in Finland and elsewhere), so most of ALLFED's research and advice would not otherwise come soon. 0.75 (0.5 to 0.95), our judgment, a little above the 0.7 the nuclear peers' arms-control work gets, in a field with more groups.

rows.explainer: ALLFED's share of all resources behind the work (Convention 2): its own $1.02M, beside its 61 volunteers (Part I line 6; at about 4 hours a week for 46 weeks at $25 an hour, about $0.28M), its president's unpaid time (54 hours a week, Part VII, no pay from ALLFED: at about $50 an hour for 50 weeks, about $0.135M), academic co-authors' time and the government staff in its workshops (about $0.2M, our judgment), so about 1.02 ÷ (1.02 + 0.28 + 0.135 + 0.2) = 0.62. 0.62 (0.45 to 0.85), our judgment; the low end if volunteers give a day a week, the high end if partners' time is small.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Whether other funders of food-resilience work would give less if small donors gave more is the room factor of @next_dollar.allfed (docs/normalization.md 2.10), so it isn't asked again here (one question per adjustment): 1, our judgment, as for every catastrophic-risk model; 0.85 to 1.05 for funging the room factor misses.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: Thin, both branches: no outcome of ALLFED's work on the deaths in a catastrophe is measured (no plan has been tested in one); the cut per dollar is a typical project's from Rethink Priorities' model and the chances are forecasts, so the shared missing-data step applies (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Benefits not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Good beyond the catastrophes counted, each a share of the modelled value: the same food work after a volcanic winter, since a magnitude-7 eruption has about a one-in-six chance this century (Cassidy and Mani 2022, Nature, https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-022-02177-x) and could cut harvests like a regional nuclear war, 13%; nuclear wars that kill fewer than 10% of people (Xia et al.'s smallest war starves 260 million, 3.5% of people), which have no shared forecast, 5%; the loss-of-industry work in other_cost_share (10% of the cost), 4%; help with ordinary food shocks (Argentina's plans for droughts as well as catastrophes), 3%. 25% (5% to 60%) in all, our judgment, above the nuclear peers' 10% because ALLFED's food work serves every sun-blocking catastrophe, not only war.

rows.label: Harm: speeding up dangerous technology, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: ALLFED's research is on foods and food systems, not on any dangerous technology. 0 (−2% to 0), our judgment.

rows.label: Harm: making nuclear war seem survivable, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Preparing to feed people after a nuclear war could, in principle, make leaders or publics treat a war as more survivable, the moral hazard often raised against civil defence; and the work publishes no threat analysis that shows a path to a weapon. −2% (−10% to 0), our judgment: the work is little known among decision-makers on war, and the deaths it describes argue for prevention.
